Chapter 5: Setting Boundaries and Seeking Support
Let’s take a look at something that can feel both empowering and a little scary—setting healthy boundaries. If you’ve spent years in an abusive relationship, the idea of saying “no” or standing up for yourself might feel not just uncomfortable, but almost impossible. Maybe you’ve learned to doubt your own instincts, or you worry that your needs don’t really matter.
Picture a young parent who’s just left a relationship filled with constant criticism. She finds it tough to speak up to her own family, afraid that saying what she really feels will make her seem selfish or ungrateful. But over time, she learns that taking care of herself isn’t just okay—it’s absolutely necessary. She starts small: saying no to invitations that feel overwhelming, asking for help when she needs it, and refusing to dive into arguments that only leave her exhausted.
Most of us don’t realize how often we put our own needs aside just to keep the peace. It’s a habit that can be tough to break, especially if you’ve spent years being told your feelings don’t matter. But here’s something important: setting boundaries isn’t about being rude or pushing people away. It’s about respecting yourself—honoring what you need to stay healthy and whole.
Support is another key ingredient in the healing journey. So many survivors feel completely alone, convinced that nobody could possibly understand what they’ve been through. But reaching out—to a therapist, a support group, or even an online community—can change everything. Suddenly, you’re not alone. You’re with people who get it, who listen, and who offer encouragement when you need it most.
One woman joined a support group for survivors of domestic violence and was amazed by the comfort she found in hearing others’ stories. She realized that her feelings of shame and self-doubt weren’t just hers; others felt the same way. That group became a lifeline, helping her set boundaries she never thought possible and start rebuilding her life.
Of course, not everyone in your life will understand or support your healing journey. Some friends or family members might downplay what happened, give advice that isn’t helpful, or even take the abuser’s side. That hurts—but it’s also a reminder: boundaries aren’t just for strangers; sometimes, you need them most with the people closest to you.
Letting go of toxic relationships is often part of the process. It might mean stepping back from folks who don’t support you, or cutting ties with those who continue to cause pain. It’s never easy, but it creates space for healthier, more fulfilling connections to grow.
Trust is another thing that often needs to be rebuilt. After betrayal or manipulation, it’s natural to feel cautious—maybe even suspicious. Many survivors struggle to believe that anyone could truly be kind or trustworthy. But here’s the good news: with time, and with the support of safe, caring people, trust can grow again.
There’s a story of a woman who, after years of isolation, started volunteering at a local community center. At first, she was nervous, wondering if she’d ever fit in. But as she got to know the other volunteers, she started to feel a sense of belonging and purpose. These new relationships helped her see that not everyone was out to hurt her—and that she was absolutely capable of building healthy, supportive connections.
Setting boundaries and seeking support aren’t things you do just once—they’re ongoing. There will be setbacks, and some days will feel harder than others. But every little step forward is a win. With patience and persistence, you can create a life that’s safe, rewarding, and truly free from the shadows of the past.
